title: Warehouses, data lakes, OLAP, batch vs stream processing
scopeHtml: Scope: OLTP vs OLAP, column stores, ETL/ELT, lakehouse, batch vs stream. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: OLTP vs OLAP
notes.html:
OLTP (online transaction processing) serves the live app: many tiny reads and writes by key. OLAP (online analytical processing) answers big questions over lots of history: few queries, each scanning millions or billions of rows.

OLTP OLAP
Example "Place order 123", "get user 42" "Revenue by city by week for 2 years"
Query touches 1 to 100 rows Millions to billions of rows, few columns
Latency goal ms seconds to minutes
Storage layout Row-oriented Column-oriented
Schema Normalized Denormalized (star schema)
Systems Postgres, MySQL, DynamoDB Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse

Running heavy analytics on the production OLTP database hurts customers: a 5-minute scan evicts cache, takes locks or I/O, and spikes latency. So you copy data to a separate analytical system.

Worked example. A 2 TB orders table. OLTP query by order id reads one 8 KB page: 1 ms. OLAP query "average order value per city for last 12 months" needs 3 columns of 500M rows. Row store reads all 2 TB; column store reads only the needed columns, about 60 GB compressed to maybe 15 GB, a 100x or more reduction in I/O.

Industry examples. Uber, Airbnb and Netflix all separate serving databases from analytical warehouses; Postgres teams offload reports to a read replica first, then to a warehouse.

Everyday analogy. A cashier serves one customer at a time quickly (OLTP); the accountant reviews the whole year's receipts in the back office (OLAP). You do not make the accountant work at the checkout counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Running reporting queries on the primary.
  • Believing one database can do both well at large scale (HTAP systems exist, such as TiDB and SingleStore, but with trade-offs).

notes.title: Column stores and the warehouse
notes.html:
A column store keeps each column's values together on disk instead of each row's. Analytics usually reads few columns of many rows, so reading only those columns saves huge I/O.

Row store (page holds whole rows):
 [1, Mumbai, 250][2, Delhi, 400][3, Mumbai, 120] ...

Column store (each column in its own file/block):
 id:    1, 2, 3 ...
 city:  Mumbai, Delhi, Mumbai ...   -> compresses extremely well
 amount:250, 400, 120 ...

Why it is fast:

  • Read only needed columns.
  • Compression: similar values compress 5x to 10x or more (dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, delta, bit-packing).
  • Vectorized execution: process batches of thousands of values with CPU SIMD.
  • Zone maps / min-max per block: skip blocks that cannot match WHERE date > ....
  • Partitioning and clustering/sort keys: prune whole partitions (for example by date).

Why it is slow for OLTP: updating one row means touching every column file; single-row lookups read blocks of many rows. Warehouses prefer bulk loads and appends.

Modern cloud warehouses separate storage and compute. Data lives in cheap object storage (S3/GCS, columnar files); compute clusters spin up on demand, scale independently and can be shared or paused. Snowflake (virtual warehouses), BigQuery (serverless slots, charged per TB scanned or by slots), Redshift (RA3 nodes with managed storage), Databricks SQL.

Star schema. A central fact table (events: orders with measures like amount, quantity and foreign keys) surrounded by dimension tables (customer, product, date, city). Queries join the big fact table to small dimensions and aggregate.

SELECT d.month, c.city, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_orders f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE d.year = 2026
GROUP BY d.month, c.city;

Worked example. BigQuery on-demand pricing is about $6.25 per TB scanned (confirm current price). A query selecting 3 columns from a table partitioned by date and filtered to one month scans maybe 20 GB (about $0.12); SELECT * over the whole table scans 5 TB (about $31). That is why partition filters and column selection matter.

Industry examples. Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse (used by Cloudflare and Uber for logs and analytics), Apache Druid and Pinot (low-latency real-time OLAP, used by LinkedIn and Uber for user-facing analytics).

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed warehouse is moderately reversible if you keep raw data in open formats (Parquet) in your own object store; locking everything inside a vendor format is harder to leave. Modeling (star schema, partitioning keys) is the long-lived decision.

Everyday analogy. A spreadsheet where you can read the whole "price" column in one go, instead of paging through every row card by card.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that warehouses are bad at single-row updates and high-concurrency point reads.
  • SELECT * on columnar engines.
  • No partition pruning, scanning years of data for a daily report.

notes.title: ETL, ELT and data pipelines
notes.html:
A pipeline moves data from sources (OLTP databases, event streams, SaaS tools) into the warehouse or lake and shapes it for analysis.

  • ETL: Extract, Transform, then Load; transformation happens on a separate engine (Spark, Informatica) before the warehouse. Older, good when the warehouse is expensive or data must be cleaned or masked first.
  • ELT: Extract, Load raw data, Transform inside the warehouse with SQL (dbt). Standard today because warehouses are cheap and elastic and you keep raw data for reprocessing.

Layers (the "medallion" or raw/staging/mart pattern):

  1. Raw/bronze: exact copy as landed (append only).
  2. Cleaned/silver: deduplicated, typed, conformed.
  3. Marts/gold: business-ready aggregates and star schemas.

Getting data out of OLTP:

  • Batch extract (nightly dump or incremental by updated_at): simple, misses hard deletes.
  • CDC (Debezium reading the WAL/binlog into Kafka): near real-time, captures deletes and every change.
  • Events published by services (clickstream, Kafka topics).

Orchestration: Airflow, Dagster or Prefect run DAGs with schedules, retries and dependencies; dbt manages SQL models and tests; data quality checks (row counts, null rates, freshness) gate downstream jobs.

# Airflow DAG sketch: nightly load then transform
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from datetime import datetime
with DAG("daily_orders", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), schedule="0 2 * * *", catchup=False) as dag:
    load = BashOperator(task_id="load_raw", bash_command="python load_orders.py {{ ds }}")
    build = BashOperator(task_id="dbt_run", bash_command="dbt run --select marts.orders")
    load >> build

Idempotency matters. A rerun for the same day must not double-count. Load into a date partition and overwrite that partition, or MERGE by key. Late-arriving data: reprocess a window (for example last 3 days) every run.

Slowly changing dimensions (SCD). When a customer's city changes, SCD Type 2 keeps history by adding a new row with valid_from, valid_to, so last year's revenue is attributed to the old city.

Worked example. 300 GB/day of events. Landing as Parquet partitioned by dt=2026-11-09 costs ~$0.023/GB-month in S3 (about $7/day of new storage growth if kept in Standard). Nightly dbt build reads yesterday's partition (300 GB, 12 min on a medium warehouse), writes marts of 2 GB.

Industry examples. Airbnb (created Airflow), Netflix (Maestro, Iceberg), Uber (Hudi originated there), Spotify and Stitch Fix with dbt, Fivetran/Airbyte for managed connectors.

Decision gravity. Keeping raw data lets you change transformations later (reversible); transforming and discarding raw data is a one-way door. Schema changes upstream (renamed column) silently break pipelines, so use data contracts and tests.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen prep line: deliveries arrive (extract), are stored raw in the pantry (load), then washed, chopped and cooked to order (transform).

Common interview traps.

  • Non-idempotent jobs that double-count on retry.
  • Incremental loads by updated_at that miss deletes.
  • No freshness or quality monitoring, so dashboards quietly show stale numbers.

notes.title: Data lakes and the lakehouse
notes.html:
A data lake stores raw data of any shape (JSON, CSV, logs, Parquet, images) cheaply in object storage, to be read by many engines later ("schema on read"). A warehouse enforces structure on write ("schema on write").

Problem with a plain lake: it is just files. No ACID transactions, no easy updates/deletes (GDPR), no schema evolution, small-file problem, readers may see half-written data. It becomes a "data swamp".

Lakehouse table formats add a transaction log and metadata over Parquet files in object storage:

  • Apache Iceberg (Netflix origin), Delta Lake (Databricks), Apache Hudi (Uber origin).
  • Features: ACID commits, snapshot isolation, time travel (SELECT ... AS OF), schema evolution, row-level updates/deletes/upserts, hidden partitioning, compaction of small files.
  • Multiple engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, BigQuery) can read the same tables.

File format choice: Parquet (columnar, compressed, the default for analytics) and ORC; Avro (row-based, good for Kafka and schema evolution); JSON/CSV only as raw landing.

Layout (Hive-style partitions):
s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-11-09/part-0001.parquet
s3://lake/orders/dt=2026-11-09/part-0002.parquet
Target file size: 128 MB to 1 GB. Thousands of 1 MB files = slow listing and planning.

Worked example. 1 PB lake in S3 Standard: 1,000,000 GB x $0.023 = $23,000/month; a comparable managed warehouse storage would cost more and tie you to one vendor. Compaction job merges 20,000 small files of 5 MB into 100 files of 1 GB, cutting query planning from 40 s to 3 s.

Industry examples. Netflix Iceberg tables on S3, Uber Hudi for upserts from CDC, Databricks lakehouse (Delta), Apple and Adobe on Iceberg, AWS Athena or Trino querying S3 directly.

Decision gravity. Warehouse for BI-heavy teams with SQL needs and low ops tolerance; lake/lakehouse for ML, unstructured data, multi-engine access and cost at petabyte scale. Open formats keep exit options (reversible). Many companies run both: lake as raw/system of record, warehouse for curated marts.

Everyday analogy. A lake is a big storeroom where you dump boxes of everything; a table format is the inventory ledger that tells you what is in which box and which boxes are current.

Common interview traps.

  • Dumping data in S3 with no catalog or schema, creating a swamp.
  • The small-files problem (millions of tiny Parquet files).
  • Ignoring deletes/GDPR on an append-only lake.

notes.title: Batch vs stream processing
notes.html:
Batch processes a large bounded dataset at intervals (hourly, nightly). Stream processes events continuously as they arrive (seconds or less).

Batch Stream
Data Bounded (yesterday's files) Unbounded (events forever)
Latency Minutes to hours Milliseconds to seconds
Throughput efficiency Very high Lower per record
Complexity Lower Higher (state, time, ordering, failures)
Examples Daily revenue report, ML training Fraud detection, live dashboards, alerts
Tools Spark, Hive, dbt, MapReduce Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming, Beam

Choose by the required freshness, not by fashion. Hourly freshness is often enough, and batch is cheaper and simpler.

Stream concepts senior interviews expect:

  • Event time vs processing time. Events arrive late or out of order (a phone offline in a tunnel). Use event timestamps.
  • Windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping, e.g. every 1 min), sliding (overlapping), session (gap-based).
  • Watermarks: the engine's estimate "no events older than T will arrive"; closes windows, with an allowed lateness for stragglers.
  • State: counts, joins and dedup need state, kept locally (RocksDB in Flink) and checkpointed to durable storage.
  • Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once (checkpointing plus transactional or idempotent sinks; Kafka transactions).
  • Backpressure: slow consumers must push back instead of crashing.
-- Flink SQL: orders per city per minute (tumbling window on event time)
SELECT city,
       TUMBLE_START(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS minute,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY city, TUMBLE(event_time, INTERVAL '1' MINUTE);

Worked example. Fraud check on card payments must decide within 200 ms: a stream job keeps a per-card 10-minute sliding count in state (about 1 KB per active card; 5M active cards = 5 GB state, sharded over 10 task slots). Nightly batch job recomputes models on 90 days of history (50 TB) and publishes updated thresholds.

Architectures.

  • Lambda: run batch and speed (stream) layers in parallel and merge at query time. Accurate but two codebases.
  • Kappa: everything is a stream; reprocess by replaying the log (Kafka with long retention). One codebase, needs a replayable log.
  • Streaming ingestion into a lakehouse (Flink or Spark writing Iceberg/Hudi) blends both: minutes of freshness, one storage layer.

Industry examples. LinkedIn built Kafka and Samza; Uber uses Flink and Pinot for live ops metrics; Netflix uses Flink for real-time recommendations and monitoring; Alibaba runs Flink at Singles' Day scale (billions of events/s reported); Spark remains dominant for batch ETL at most companies.

Decision gravity. Stream processing is a long-term operational commitment (state, upgrades, reprocessing). Start batch unless a product requirement (fraud, alerts, live UI) needs seconds. Moving batch to stream later is possible if sources are in Kafka and logic is idempotent; the reverse is easy.

Everyday analogy. Batch is doing all laundry on Sunday; streaming is washing each shirt the moment it gets dirty. Weekly laundry is more efficient; a pilot's shirt may need the second approach.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing streaming when daily batch meets the requirement.
  • Ignoring late and out-of-order events.
  • Claiming "exactly-once" end to end without idempotent or transactional sinks.
  • Forgetting how to reprocess history after a bug fix.

notes.title: Putting it together: an analytics architecture
notes.html:
A sensible end-to-end design for an e-commerce company at about 50M orders/year and 500M clickstream events/day:

  1. OLTP Postgres/MySQL for orders (sharded or not by size), DynamoDB for carts.
  2. CDC via Debezium into Kafka (8 to 24 partitions per big topic, 7 days retention); apps also publish clickstream events directly.
  3. Lake sink: Kafka Connect or Flink writes Parquet/Iceberg into S3, partitioned by dt and hour.
  4. Warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift) loads curated data; dbt builds star schemas daily and key marts hourly.
  5. Real-time layer: Flink aggregates for live dashboards and alerts, serving via Pinot/ClickHouse or Redis.
  6. Serving: BI tool (Looker, Superset), notebooks, ML feature store.
  7. Governance: catalog (DataHub, Glue), access control, PII masking, retention rules (GDPR deletion), lineage and data-quality tests.

Worked example (storage). 500M events/day x 500 bytes = 250 GB/day raw JSON; Parquet with compression is about 5x smaller: 50 GB/day, 18 TB/year, about $420/month in S3 Standard after one year of accumulation (18,000 GB x $0.023), and cheaper with tiering.

Cost levers. Partition and cluster tables, materialized aggregates, auto-suspend compute, cap runaway queries (BigQuery maximum_bytes_billed), tier old data to cold storage, and avoid duplicate copies.

Decision gravity. Each layer has an exit: raw events in open formats can be re-ingested into any warehouse. The commitment that is hardest to undo is business definitions ("what is an active user") scattered in dashboards; centralize them in a semantic layer or dbt models.

Industry examples. Common stacks: Fivetran/Airbyte + Snowflake + dbt + Looker; Kafka + Flink + Iceberg + Trino; Uber's Kafka + Hudi + Presto + Pinot.

Everyday analogy. A city's water system: reservoirs (lake), treatment plant (transform), taps for drinking (BI) and a fast pipe for firefighters (real-time).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every tool without justifying freshness and volume numbers.
  • Forgetting governance (PII, retention, access).
  • No plan for backfills and reprocessing.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• OLTP serves the app by key; OLAP scans history. Keep them on separate systems.
  • Column stores read only needed columns, compress well and vectorize; warehouses separate storage from compute; model with star schemas and prune partitions.
  • ELT with raw, cleaned and mart layers; make jobs idempotent, use CDC for deletes, test data quality, keep raw data.
  • Data lakes hold open-format files in object storage; Iceberg/Delta/Hudi add ACID, time travel and updates; fight small files.
  • Batch for hours-fresh and cheap; stream for seconds-fresh, with event time, windows, watermarks, state and delivery semantics.
  • Combine them (CDC, Kafka, lake, warehouse, real-time OLAP) based on freshness needs and cost, with governance built in.
